claim: INAVA (C1ORF106) was identified as a risk factor for chronic inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) by genome-wide association studies and targeted exome sequencing.
source: C1ORF106, recently named INAVA (Innate Immune Activator), was identified as a risk factor for the chronic inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) by genome-wide association studies and targeted exome sequencing (Rivas et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rivas et al., 2011, which is a reference to published scholarly work.

claim: Mice lacking INAVA show defects in intestinal barrier integrity at steady state.
source: Mice lacking the protein altogether show defects in intestinal barrier integrity at steady state and greater susceptibility to mucosal infection (Mohanan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mohanan et al., 2018.

claim: Mice lacking INAVA show greater susceptibility to mucosal infection.
source: Mice lacking the protein altogether show defects in intestinal barrier integrity at steady state and greater susceptibility to mucosal infection (Mohanan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mohanan et al., 2018.

claim: Human macrophages carrying the IBD rs7554511 risk allele have decreased INAVA expression.
source: Human macrophages carrying the IBD rs7554511 risk allele have decreased INAVA expression and show multiple defects in myeloid function, including in innate immune NOD2 signaling and cytokine secretion, and in microbial clearance in association with reduced autophagy and ROS production (Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yan et al., 2017.

claim: Human macrophages carrying the IBD rs7554511 risk allele show defects in innate immune NOD2 signaling.
source: Human macrophages carrying the IBD rs7554511 risk allele have decreased INAVA expression and show multiple defects in myeloid function, including in innate immune NOD2 signaling and cytokine secretion, and in microbial clearance in association with reduced autophagy and ROS production (Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yan et al., 2017.

claim: Human macrophages carrying the IBD rs7554511 risk allele show defects in cytokine secretion.
source: Human macrophages carrying the IBD rs7554511 risk allele have decreased INAVA expression and show multiple defects in myeloid function, including in innate immune NOD2 signaling and cytokine secretion, and in microbial clearance in association with reduced autophagy and ROS production (Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yan et al., 2017.

claim: Human macrophages carrying the IBD rs7554511 risk allele show defects in microbial clearance in association with reduced autophagy and ROS production.
source: Human macrophages carrying the IBD rs7554511 risk allele have decreased INAVA expression and show multiple defects in myeloid function, including in innate immune NOD2 signaling and cytokine secretion, and in microbial clearance in association with reduced autophagy and ROS production (Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yan et al., 2017.

claim: INAVA is strongly enriched in simple epithelial cells.
source: We previously determined that INAVA is strongly enriched in simple epithelial cells (Nelms et al., 2016) - the cell type that forms mucosal barriers.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nelms et al., 2016.

claim: INAVA has a single distinguishing feature, the Domain of Unknown Function DUF3338 (renamed CUPID).
source: By domain analysis, the molecule has a single distinguishing feature, the Domain of Unknown Function DUF3338 (which we rename CUPID for Cytohesin Ubiquitin Protein Inducing Domain).
evidence: The claim is based on domain analysis performed by the authors.

claim: Three other human proteins contain CUPID: FRMD4a, FRMD4B, and CCDC120.
source: Three other human proteins contain CUPID: FRMD4a, FRMD4B, and CCDC120, and two are implicated in human disease (Cappola et al., 2010; Fine et al., 2015; Garner et al., 2014; Goldie et al., 2012; Lambert et al., 2013; Velcheti et al., 2017; Yoon et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Two CUPID-containing proteins are implicated in human disease.
source: Three other human proteins contain CUPID: FRMD4a, FRMD4B, and CCDC120, and two are implicated in human disease (Cappola et al., 2010; Fine et al., 2015; Garner et al., 2014; Goldie et al., 2012; Lambert et al., 2013; Velcheti et al., 2017; Yoon et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: All CUPID-containing proteins appear to bind the ARF-GEF cytohesin family members.
source: All appear to bind the ARF-GEF (guanine nucleotide-exchange factors) cytohesin family members (Huttlin et al., 2017; Ikenouchi and Umeda, 2010; Klarlund et al., 2001; Mohanan et al., 2018; Torii et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cytohesins are guanine nucleotide-exchange factors for the ARF-family of proteins (ARF 1–4).
source: The cytohesins are guanine nucleotide-exchange factors for the ARF-family of proteins (ARF 1–4), which regulate cell membrane and F-actin dynamics (Donaldson and Jackson, 2011; Stalder and Antonny, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Donaldson and Jackson, 2011 and Stalder and Antonny, 2013.

claim: ARF proteins regulate cell membrane and F-actin dynamics.
source: The cytohesins are guanine nucleotide-exchange factors for the ARF-family of proteins (ARF 1–4), which regulate cell membrane and F-actin dynamics (Donaldson and Jackson, 2011; Stalder and Antonny, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Donaldson and Jackson, 2011 and Stalder and Antonny, 2013.

claim: All cytohesins contain a N-terminal coiled-coil (CC) protein-protein interaction region, an enzymatic SEC7 guanine nucleotide-exchange factor (GEF) domain, and a C-terminal PIP-binding PH domain.
source: All cytohesins contain a N-terminal coiled-coil (CC) protein-protein interaction region, an enzymatic SEC7 guanine nucleotide-exchange factor (GEF) domain, and a C-terminal PIP-binding PH domain.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about cytohesin structure.

claim: In their inactive conformation, cytohesins localize to the cytosol.
source: In their inactive conformation, the cytohesins localize to the cytosol.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about cytohesin localization.

claim: Full-blown GEF activation of ARNO requires membrane recruitment via ARNO binding to PIP2.
source: Full-blown GEF activation, typified by cytohesin 2 (also known as ARNO), requires membrane recruitment via ARNO binding to PIP2 (phosphatidylinositol 4, 5-bisphosphate), and then (activated) ARF-GTP, a product of the ARNO-GEF reaction (Chardin et al., 1996; Cohen et al., 2007; Malaby et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chardin et al., 1996; Cohen et al., 2007; Malaby et al., 2013.

claim: Full-blown GEF activation of ARNO requires binding to ARF-GTP, a product of the ARNO-GEF reaction.
source: Full-blown GEF activation, typified by cytohesin 2 (also known as ARNO), requires membrane recruitment via ARNO binding to PIP2 (phosphatidylinositol 4, 5-bisphosphate), and then (activated) ARF-GTP, a product of the ARNO-GEF reaction (Chardin et al., 1996; Cohen et al., 2007; Malaby et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chardin et al., 1996; Cohen et al., 2007; Malaby et al., 2013.

claim: ARNO activation enables an enzymatically-driven positive feedback-loop for rapidly amplifying a localized pool of activated cytohesins and ARF-GTP.
source: This enables an enzymatically-driven positive feedback-loop for rapidly amplifying a localized pool of activated cytohesins and ARF-GTP needed to drive the massive ARF-dependent changes in actin and membrane dynamics that underlie cell spreading and epithelial breakdown (Santy and Casanova, 2001; Stalder et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Santy and Casanova, 2001; Stalder et al., 2011.

claim: Caco2BBe cells lacking INAVA show enhanced cell spreading.
source: Caco2BBe cells lacking INAVA show enhanced cell spreading, while cells stably expressing INAVA-GFP are similar to wild type (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: Caco2BBe cells stably expressing INAVA-GFP are similar to wild type in cell spreading.
source: Caco2BBe cells lacking INAVA show enhanced cell spreading, while cells stably expressing INAVA-GFP are similar to wild type (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: INAVA-deficient Caco2BBe cells display increased permeability to 4 kDa FITC dextran.
source: When grown on permeable supports as polarized monolayers, INAVA-deficient cells display increased permeability to 4 kDa FITC dextran and reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F), implicating defects in paracellular permeability and intercellular junctions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: INAVA-deficient Caco2BBe cells display reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER).
source: When grown on permeable supports as polarized monolayers, INAVA-deficient cells display increased permeability to 4 kDa FITC dextran and reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F), implicating defects in paracellular permeability and intercellular junctions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: INAVA-deficient cells have defects in paracellular permeability and intercellular junctions.
source: When grown on permeable supports as polarized monolayers, INAVA-deficient cells display increased permeability to 4 kDa FITC dextran and reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F), implicating defects in paracellular permeability and intercellular junctions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the increased permeability and reduced TEER measurements.

claim: Caco2BBe monolayers that overexpress INAVA exhibit increased integrity of intercellular junctions as measured by higher TEER.
source: Conversely, Caco2BBe monolayers that overexpress INAVA exhibit evidence of increased integrity of intercellular junctions as measured by higher TEER and greater tolerance to depletion of intercellular adherens junctions caused by exposure to low Ca2+ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Caco2BBe monolayers that overexpress INAVA exhibit greater tolerance to depletion of intercellular adherens junctions caused by exposure to low Ca2+.
source: Conversely, Caco2BBe monolayers that overexpress INAVA exhibit evidence of increased integrity of intercellular junctions as measured by higher TEER and greater tolerance to depletion of intercellular adherens junctions caused by exposure to low Ca2+ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: INAVA knock-out mice support a role for INAVA in maintenance of intercellular epithelial junctions responsible for mucosal barrier function.
source: These phenotypes are consistent with a recent study using INAVA knock-out mice that supports a role for INAVA in maintenance of intercellular epithelial junctions responsible for mucosal barrier function (Mohanan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mohanan et al., 2018.

claim: Humans express two isoforms of INAVA.
source: Humans express two isoforms of INAVA. The short-isoform (INAVA-S) lacks a 99-amino-acid segment N-terminal to CUPID (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The short-isoform (INAVA-S) lacks a 99-amino-acid segment N-terminal to CUPID.
source: Humans express two isoforms of INAVA. The short-isoform (INAVA-S) lacks a 99-amino-acid segment N-terminal to CUPID (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Both long INAVA-GFP and short INAVA-S-GFP isoforms localized to cell-cell contacts.
source: Both long INAVA-GFP and short INAVA-S-GFP isoforms localized to cell-cell contacts (Figure 1C,D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Leading edges of migratory cells were uniformly devoid of INAVA.
source: Notably, leading edges of migratory cells were uniformly devoid of INAVA.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data.

claim: In well-differentiated polarized Caco2BBe monolayers, INAVA localized to tight and adherens junctions.
source: In well-differentiated polarized Caco2BBe monolayers, INAVA localized to tight and adherens junctions, as evidenced by co-localization with E-cadherin and ZO-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I,J.

claim: The C-terminal region flanking the INAVA-CUPID domain (aa 261–677) localized to lateral membranes when expressed on its own.
source: When expressed on its own, the C-terminal region flanking the INAVA-CUPID domain (aa 261–677) also localized to lateral membranes (Figure 1D, bottom panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The CUPID domain on its own localized to the cytosol.
source: The CUPID domain on its own localized to the cytosol, and the CUPID domain together with the N-terminal flanking region (aa 1–260) localized to cytosolic puncta (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The CUPID domain together with the N-terminal flanking region (aa 1–260) localized to cytosolic puncta.
source: The CUPID domain on its own localized to the cytosol, and the CUPID domain together with the N-terminal flanking region (aa 1–260) localized to cytosolic puncta (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The C-terminal region of INAVA is necessary and sufficient for lateral membrane targeting.
source: Thus, the C-terminal region of INAVA is necessary and sufficient for lateral membrane targeting.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the localization data of INAVA constructs.

claim: Lateral membrane localization of INAVA did not depend upon association with the E-cadherin complex.
source: Lateral membrane localization did not depend upon association with the E-cadherin complex. This was evidenced in cells treated with 6 mM EGTA to disassemble adherens junctions and induce E-cadherin endocytosis. While E-cadherin localized to endocytic vesicles upon EGTA treatment, INAVA remained at lateral membranes (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Upon EGTA treatment, E-cadherin localized to endocytic vesicles while INAVA remained at lateral membranes.
source: This was evidenced in cells treated with 6 mM EGTA to disassemble adherens junctions and induce E-cadherin endocytosis. While E-cadherin localized to endocytic vesicles upon EGTA treatment, INAVA remained at lateral membranes (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ZO-1 staining remained unchanged upon EGTA treatment.
source: Staining for the tight junction protein ZO-1 as a control also remained unchanged.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: INAVA localizes to lateral membranes independently of E-cadherin.
source: Thus, INAVA localizes to lateral membranes independently of E-cadherin.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the EGTA treatment experiment.

claim: INAVA plays a critical role in maintaining or regulating epithelial barrier integrity.
source: Overall, these results support a critical role for INAVA in maintaining or regulating epithelial barrier integrity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective experimental results.

claim: INAVA-CUPID (aa 100–261) assembled with cytohesin 1, cytohesin 2 (ARNO), and cytohesin 3 (GRP1) in a yeast-based protein-protein interaction platform.
source: We first screened the cytohesins 1–3 for binding to INAVA-CUPID (aa 100–261) using a yeast-based protein-protein interaction platform (Schmitz et al., 2009). In all cases, as evidenced by intracellular puncta formation, CUPID assembled with each of the cytohesins: cytohesin 1, cytohesin 2 (ARNO), and cytohesin 3 (GRP1), (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Coiled-coil domains of the cytohesins were sufficient for direct interaction with CUPID.
source: Coiled-coil domains of the cytohesins were sufficient for direct interaction with CUPID.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data.

claim: Recombinant INAVA-CUPID was sufficient to pull down the coiled-coil domains of Cytohesin-1, ARNO, and GRP1.
source: In a purified system, recombinant INAVA-CUPID was sufficient to pull down the coiled-coil domains of Cytohesin-1, ARNO, and GRP1 (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cytohesin binding by INAVA is direct and dependent upon CUPID.
source: Thus, cytohesin binding by INAVA is direct and dependent upon CUPID.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pulldown experiments.

claim: CUPID binding to the coiled-coil regions of the cytohesins did not affect their GEF activity.
source: CUPID binding to the coiled-coil regions of the cytohesins, however, did not affect their GEF activity, as assessed biochemically using recombinant proteins in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Caco2BBe cells stably expressing myc-tagged ARNO or GRP1 rapidly suppressed ARNO and GRP1 expression.
source: To test how INAVA may affect cytohesin function, we generated Caco2BBe intestinal cells stably expressing myc-tagged ARNO or GRP1. These cells, however, rapidly suppressed ARNO and GRP1 expression, as evidenced by the lack of protein detected upon transduction.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: PMA rescued ARNO and GRP1 protein expression in Caco2BBe cells by overcoming endogenous mechanism(s) of epigenetic gene silencing.
source: PMA (phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate), which strongly activates the CMV promotors used in these transductions, rescued ARNO and GRP1 protein expression, presumably by overcoming the endogenous mechanism(s) of epigenetic gene silencing operating in these cell lines (Figure 2B, compare lanes 1 and 3; and lanes 5 and 7) (Löser et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and a citation to Löser et al., 1998.

claim: INAVA rescued ARNO expression in the absence of PMA when co-expressed in the same cells.
source: Strikingly, when co-expressed in the same cells, INAVA rescued ARNO expression in the absence of PMA (Figure 2B, compare lanes 1 and 2), implicating a stabilizing interaction between the two proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: INAVA did not rescue the cytohesin GRP1 against gene-suppression.
source: The effect was specific to ARNO as INAVA did not rescue the cytohesin GRP1 against gene-suppression (compare lanes 5 and 6).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data comparing lanes 5 and 6.

claim: Over-expression of INAVA-GFP increased endogenous ARNO protein levels.
source: Over-expression of INAVA-GFP increased endogenous ARNO protein levels with no apparent changes in TEER or paracellular flux when compared to wildtype cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Two independently created INAVA KO Caco2BBe cell lines showed no evidence for increased ARNO levels.
source: Two independently created INAVA KO Caco2BBe cell lines showed no evidence for increased ARNO levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), unlike the results recently reported for INAVA's effect on cytohesin 1, a closely related ARF-GEF member of the cytohesin family.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: INAVA induces the ubiquitin-dependent degradation of the cytohesins according to a recent report.
source: Two independently created INAVA KO Caco2BBe cell lines showed no evidence for increased ARNO levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), unlike the results recently reported for INAVA's effect on cytohesin 1, a closely related ARF-GEF member of the cytohesin family. In accord with these results, we found durable expression of ARNO in primary human macrophages over-expressing INAVA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G). Thus, INAVA interacts with and appears to stabilize ARNO expression in intact cells, consistent with our biochemical data, but in contrast to a recent report that INAVA induces the ubiquitin-dependent degradation of the cytohesins (Mohanan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mohanan et al., 2018.

claim: INAVA interacts with and appears to stabilize ARNO expression in intact cells.
source: Thus, INAVA interacts with and appears to stabilize ARNO expression in intact cells, consistent with our biochemical data, but in contrast to a recent report that INAVA induces the ubiquitin-dependent degradation of the cytohesins (Mohanan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing increased ARNO levels with INAVA expression.

claim: Upon induction with doxycycline, ARNO localized to the cytosol in Caco2BBe cells.
source: Upon induction with dox, ARNO localized to the cytosol, consistent with the molecule folding in an auto-inhibited inactive state (Figure 2C top panels) (Cohen et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and a citation to Cohen et al., 2007.

claim: Co-expression of INAVA-GFP recruited ARNO to lateral membranes.
source: Co-expression of INAVA-GFP recruited ARNO to lateral membranes, consistent with our findings that ARNO and INAVA form stable protein complexes (Figure 2C bottom panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The INAVA-ARNO complex did not cause epithelial cell spreading or disassembly of intercellular contacts.
source: Unexpectedly, given ARNO's canonical actions in regulating F-actin assembly and membrane dynamics (Turner and Brown, 2001), the INAVA-ARNO complex did not cause epithelial cell spreading or disassembly of intercellular contacts.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations and contrasts with expectations from the literature (Turner and Brown, 2001).

claim: Intercellular junctions remained fully intact in cells expressing INAVA-ARNO complex as assessed by TEER.
source: Intercellular junctions remained fully intact as assessed by TEER (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The INAVA-ARNO complex enhanced lateral membrane F-actin assembly.
source: We did, however, find enhancement of lateral membrane F-actin assembly (Figure 2D,E), consistent with the anticipated effects of ARF activation on cortical F-actin (Myers and Casanova, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D,E and a citation to Myers and Casanova, 2008.

claim: Cells expressing INAVA alone showed modest amplified F-actin density at lateral membranes.
source: Cells expressing INAVA alone showed modest amplified F-actin density at lateral membranes.
evidence: The claim is based on imaging data.

claim: Expression of ARNO alone had no detectable effect on lateral membrane F-actin density.
source: Expression of ARNO alone had no detectable effect.
evidence: The claim is based on imaging data.

claim: Expression of both INAVA and ARNO together strongly amplified lateral membrane cortical F-actin (>2 fold).
source: In contrast, expression of both INAVA and ARNO together strongly amplified lateral membrane cortical F-actin (>2 fold).
evidence: The claim is based on imaging data.

claim: The effects of INAVA-ARNO on F-actin assembly did not require ARF-GTP binding to ARNO or ARNO's enzymatic GEF activity.
source: Remarkably, the effects of INAVA-ARNO on F-actin assembly did not require ARF-GTP binding to ARNO or ARNO's enzymatic GEF activity (Figure 2F), as we observed the same enhanced densities of lateral membrane F-actin in Caco2BBe cells expressing the ARNO GEF mutant (E156K) or the ARF-GTP binding mutant (K366A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: ARNO mutants lacking the ability to bind PIP2 (K268A) failed to enhance F-actin.
source: In contrast, ARNO mutants lacking the ability to bind PIP2 (K268A) failed to enhance F-actin (Figure 2F, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: When complexed with INAVA, only PIP binding by ARNO is required for effecting F-actin assembly in intact cells.
source: Thus, in intact cells, when complexed with INAVA, only PIP binding by ARNO is required for effecting F-actin assembly.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mutant analysis data.

claim: In Caco2BBe cells expressing ARNO together with just the INAVA-CUPID domain, there was evidence for increased F-actin on intracellular vesicles.
source: To identify the INAVA region required for ARNO-mediated F-actin effects, we examined cortical F-actin assemblies in Caco2BBe cells expressing ARNO together with just the INAVA-CUPID domain. In this case, because CUPID alone cannot target ARNO to lateral membranes (Figure 1D), we found evidence for increased F-actin on intracellular vesicles, where both CUPID and ARNO co-localized (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: In MCF7 cells, both INAVA and ARNO colocalized on intracellular vesicles, and both proteins were required for the induction of F-actin rich vesicles.
source: This phenotype was amplified and more easily observed in human mammary epithelial MCF7 cells. In MCF7 cells, both INAVA and ARNO colocalized on intracellular vesicles, and both proteins were required for the induction of F-actin rich vesicles. Expression of each protein alone did not induce the vesicle phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I,J.

claim: The ARNO-GEF (E156K) and ARF-GTP binding (K336A) mutants promoted formation of F-actin coated vesicles in MCF7 cells.
source: The ARNO-GEF (E156K) and ARF-GTP binding (K336A) mutants also promoted formation of F-actin coated vesicles, consistent with our earlier results.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: INAVA and the ARNO PIP2-binding mutant did not promote actin assembly in MCF7 cells.
source: In contrast, as in the Caco2BBe model, INAVA and the ARNO PIP2-binding mutant did not promote actin assembly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K.

claim: The GEF and ARF-binding activities of ARNO are dispensable for F-actin assembly when bound to INAVA.
source: Thus, the GEF and ARF-binding activities of ARNO are dispensable (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1K), again implicating a unique and non-canonical mechanism of action for the cytohesins in regulating F-actin dynamics when bound to INAVA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mutant analysis data.

claim: CUPID binding to ARNO displaces the positive-feedback hyperactivation of ARFs to enable a smaller (modulated) effect on cortical F-actin assembly required for barrier integrity.
source: In other words, instead of the substantial ARNO GEF-dependent hyperactivation of ARFs leading to massive F-actin rearrangement, cell spreading, and epithelial breakdown (Stalder and Antonny, 2013; White et al., 2010), CUPID binding to ARNO displaces the positive-feedback hyperactivation of ARFs to enable instead a smaller (modulated) effect on cortical F-actin assembly, which we propose is required for barrier integrity (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data and citations to Stalder and Antonny, 2013; White et al., 2010.

claim: ARNO has been implicated in IL-1β signaling.
source: ARNO has been implicated in IL-1β signaling (Zhu et al., 2012), and given the association of INAVA with inflammatory bowel disease, we examined the effect of IL-1β on INAVA-ARNO function.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhu et al., 2012.

claim: IL-1β rapidly within 30 min induced the relocalization of INAVA-GFP from lateral membranes to cytosolic puncta in Caco2BBe cells.
source: We found that IL-1β rapidly within 30 min induced the relocalization of INAVA-GFP from lateral membranes to cytosolic puncta in Caco2BBe cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: IL-1β-induced cytosolic puncta were also found in human colon HCT8 cells with a stronger phenotype.
source: IL-1β-induced cytosolic puncta were also found in human colon HCT8 cells where we found a stronger phenotype (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: INAVA puncta were assembled from cytosolic pools of INAVA-GFP in HCT8 cells.
source: In this case, puncta were assembled from cytosolic pools of INAVA-GFP as HCT8 cells do not form intercellular junctions (Vermeulen et al., 1997) where INAVA-GFP normally localizes.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations and a citation to Vermeulen et al., 1997.

claim: IL-1β-induced INAVA-puncta were not efficiently formed in HCT8 cells lacking TRAF6.
source: INAVA puncta appeared to be associated with IL-1β signaling as IL-1β-induced INAVA-puncta were not efficiently formed in HCT8 cells lacking TRAF6 (CRISPR-Cas9 KO), the ubiquitin E3 ligase required for IL-1β signal transduction (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) (Cao et al., 1996; Lomaga et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and citations to Cao et al., 1996; Lomaga et al., 1999.

claim: TRAF6 is the ubiquitin E3 ligase required for IL-1β signal transduction.
source: INAVA puncta appeared to be associated with IL-1β signaling as IL-1β-induced INAVA-puncta were not efficiently formed in HCT8 cells lacking TRAF6 (CRISPR-Cas9 KO), the ubiquitin E3 ligase required for IL-1β signal transduction (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) (Cao et al., 1996; Lomaga et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cao et al., 1996; Lomaga et al., 1999.

claim: TNFα induced INAVA puncta to a much lower extent than IL-1β.
source: TNFα, another inflammatory cytokine, induced INAVA puncta to a much lower extent (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), suggesting selectivity for INAVA action in different inflammatory cascades.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The short INAVA-S isoform rarely induced puncta formation in Caco2BBe or HCT8 intestinal cells.
source: Notably, the short INAVA-S isoform rarely induced puncta formation in Caco2BBe or HCT8 intestinal cells (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The N-terminal region of INAVA is required for puncta formation.
source: We conclude the N-terminal region of INAVA is required for puncta formation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the short isoform lacking the N-terminal region does not form puncta.

claim: HEK293T cells expressing INAVA responded to IL-1β by enhanced NF-κB activation.
source: To test if INAVA affects IL-1β signaling, we used HEK293T cells expressing INAVA together with a NF-κB-dependent luciferase reporter. The cells were treated with IL-1β or co-transfected with TRAF6, which also induces an inflammatory response. Cells expressing INAVA responded to IL-1β or TRAF6 overexpression by enhanced NF-κB activation, as assessed using luciferase expression (Figure 3C; numerical values Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: HEK293T cells expressing INAVA responded to TRAF6 overexpression by enhanced NF-κB activation.
source: The cells were treated with IL-1β or co-transfected with TRAF6, which also induces an inflammatory response. Cells expressing INAVA responded to IL-1β or TRAF6 overexpression by enhanced NF-κB activation, as assessed using luciferase expression (Figure 3C; numerical values Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cells expressing the short INAVA-S isoform did not show enhanced NF-κB activation in response to IL-1β or TRAF6.
source: Cells expressing the short INAVA-S isoform, however, did not.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data.

claim: The short INAVA-S isoform cannot assemble into cytosolic puncta.
source: This result aligns with our finding that the short isoform cannot assemble into cytosolic puncta, further implicating puncta formation in the signaling cascade.
evidence: The claim is based on earlier experimental observations.

claim: Cells expressing INAVA lacking the CUPID domain failed to show amplified IL-1β signal transduction.
source: We also found that cells expressing INAVA lacking the CUPID domain (CUPID Δ) or cells expressing only the CUPID domain failed to show amplified IL-1β signal transduction (Figure 3D; numerical values Figure 3—source data 2).

claim: The CUPID domain is required, but not sufficient, for amplified IL-1β signal transduction.

claim: INAVA-puncta mark the formation of multiprotein signalosomes required for affecting inflammatory responses.

claim: INAVA is not essential for IL-1β induced signaling.

claim: The signalosomes mediating INAVA activity depend on the INAVA-N-terminal and CUPID domains.

claim: The signalosomes mediating INAVA activity depend on the enzymatic activity of TRAF6.

claim: HEK293T cells lacking TRAF6 failed to mediate the enhancement of IL-1β signal transduction.

evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: HEK293T cells over-expressing TRAF6 enzymatic mutant (C70A) failed to mediate the enhancement of IL-1β signal transduction.
source: This is best evidenced in HEK293T cells lacking TRAF6, or in cells over-expressing its enzymatic mutant (C70A). Both cell lines failed to mediate the enhancement of IL-1β signal transduction (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; numerical values Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ARNO over-expression blocked INAVA's activity in IL-1β signal transduction.

claim: MDMs expressing wild type INAVA responded to MDP treatment by robust activation (phosphorylation) of NF-κB and the MAP-kinases ERK, p38, and JNK.
source: Compared to MDMs transfected with empty vector (EV), MDMs expressing wild type INAVA responded to IL-1β or MDP treatment by robust activation (phosphorylation) of NF-κB and the MAP-kinases ERK, p38, and JNK (Figure 4D,E, black bars; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).

claim: MDMs expressing INAVA lacking the CUPID domain failed to respond to IL-1β and MDP treatment.

claim: Expression of ARNO blocked the IL-1β-induced, INAVA-dependent NF-κB and MAPK activation in MDMs in a dose-dependent manner.

claim: Expression of ARNO blocked the MDP-induced, INAVA-dependent NF-κB and MAPK activation in MDMs in a dose-dependent manner.

claim: Expression of ARNO blocked the IL-1β-induced, INAVA-dependent TNF secretion in MDMs in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We also found that in all cases the expression of ARNO (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–G) blocked the IL-1β- and MDP-induced, INAVA-dependent NF-κB and MAPK activation and TNF secretion in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4H, black bars; Figure 4I; Figure 4—figure supplement 1H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4H,I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–G,H,I.

claim: Primary human macrophages exhibit INAVA-ARNO mediated regulation of IL-1β signaling.

evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data in MDMs.

claim: Cells expressing both TRAF6 and INAVA exhibited much higher levels of protein ubiquitination.
source: To test this, we examined protein polyubiquitination in HEK293T cells expressing HA-tagged ubiquitin. Cells expressing both TRAF6 and INAVA exhibited much higher levels of protein ubiquitination as assessed by anti-HA immunoblot (Figure 5A, compare lane 4 with lanes 1–3).

claim: Cells expressing the short INAVA-S isoform lacked the enhanced ubiquitination response.

claim: Overexpression of ARNO strongly inhibited INAVA-TRAF6 induced ubiquitination.
source: We also found that overexpression of ARNO strongly inhibited INAVA-TRAF6 induced ubiquitination (Figure 5B, compare lane 8 with lane 6), consistent with our discovery that ARNO can act as a negative regulator in this pathway.

claim: INAVA appears to act as an enhancer of the ubiquitin-cascades induced by TRAF6.
source: Thus, INAVA appears to act as an enhancer of the ubiquitin-cascades induced by TRAF6, and this is blocked by ARNO.

claim: The INAVA-CUPID domain has activity as an enhancer of TRAF6 ubiquitination.
source: Thus, the INAVA-CUPID domain has activity as an enhancer of TRAF6 ubiquitination.

claim: The INAVA-dependent amplification of ubiquitination in vitro was fully inhibited by the addition of recombinant ARNO.
source: Notably, the INAVA-dependent amplification of ubiquitination in vitro was fully inhibited by the addition of recombinant ARNO (Figure 5D, compare lane 8 with lane 4), explaining how ARNO can act by binding INAVA to negatively regulate the inflammatory response in this pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

source: INAVA-CUPID binds ARNO, targets the molecule to lateral membranes of epithelial monolayers, and enables ARNO to affect F-actin assembly without the need for GEF activity or positive ARF-GTP feedback (Figure 2G).

claim: INAVA-CUPID enables ARNO to affect F-actin assembly without the need for GEF activity or positive ARF-GTP feedback.
